claim: Did you know… people respond to stimuli that have not yet been shown?

studies.cite: Bem (2011), Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
studies.finding: Reported nine experiments in which participants' responses appeared to be influenced by stimuli presented only after they had responded.
studies.verdict: Independent replications failed; a large preregistered test found nothing.

studies.finding: Ran three preregistered replications of Bem's retroactive recall experiment, 150 participants in total, and found no effect.
studies.verdict: Combined result was null (p = .83, one-tailed).

studies.cite: Kekecs et al. (2023), Royal Society Open Science
studies.finding: Ten laboratories in nine countries repeated Bem's first experiment with 2,115 participants under a protocol agreed with proponents.
studies.verdict: Success rate 49.89% against chance of 50%; all four tests favored the null.

claim: Did you know… volunteers can receive images telepathically while sensory-deprived?

studies.finding: Reviewed ganzfeld telepathy studies and reported receivers scoring about 35% against 25% chance, calling the effect replicable.
studies.verdict: Prompted a long dispute over methods and replicability that has not ended.

studies.finding: Pooled 30 later ganzfeld studies from seven laboratories (1,198 trials) and found no significant effect.
studies.verdict: Stouffer z = 0.70, p = .24; effect did not replicate in this set.

studies.cite: Storm, Tressoldi & Di Risio (2010), Psychological Bulletin
studies.finding: Meta-analyzed 67 free-response studies from 1992 to 2008 and reported a significant ganzfeld effect, mean effect size 0.142.
studies.verdict: Proponents' analysis found an effect; critics dispute the inclusion criteria.

claim: Did you know… human intention can bias random number generators?

studies.cite: Jahn, Dunne & Nelson (1997), Journal of Scientific Exploration
studies.finding: Reviewed a 12-year Princeton program of over 1,000 experimental series, reporting tiny shifts in random output that matched operators' stated intentions.
studies.verdict: Effects were minute and the program's results were not independently reproduced.

studies.finding: Meta-analyzed 380 random-generator studies and found a very small effect that shrank as sample size grew.
studies.verdict: Authors judged publication bias a plausible explanation; evidence 'not proven'.

claim: Did you know… random number generators worldwide drift during major world events?

studies.cite: Nelson, Radin, Shoup & Bancel (2002), Foundations of Physics Letters
studies.finding: Reported that a global network of random generators departed from chance expectation during events of broad importance, including September 11, 2001.
studies.verdict: Event selection and analysis choices were criticized; no mechanism proposed.

studies.finding: Reviewed the project's September 11 analyses and questioned the data processing, the prediction registry, and cumulative-sum plots.
studies.verdict: Rated the cogency of the results as low.

claim: Did you know… a dog can sense when its owner starts heading home?

studies.cite: Wiseman, Smith & Milton (1998), British Journal of Psychology
studies.finding: Ran four experiments testing whether the dog Jaytee signaled at the window when his owner set off for home.
studies.verdict: Signals came early or not at all; proponent's pattern called a post hoc artifact.

claim: Did you know… government-funded psychics described hidden targets better than chance?

studies.finding: Reviewed two decades of SRI and SAIC remote viewing research and concluded the results exceeded chance by wide margins.
studies.verdict: Presented as established by the author; contested by the other reviewer.

studies.finding: Evaluated the same program and argued that the conclusion was premature and that findings lacked independent replication.
studies.verdict: Called apparent consistency with other psi research possibly illusory; unresolved.

claim: Did you know… the body reacts a few seconds before a random event?

studies.cite: Mossbridge, Tressoldi & Utts (2012), Frontiers in Psychology
studies.finding: Meta-analyzed 26 reports from seven laboratories and found a small anticipatory physiological effect, effect size 0.21, before unpredictable stimuli.
studies.verdict: Authors concede flexible analyses and exclusions; independent replications are still needed.

claim: Did you know… astrologers can match a birth chart to a personality profile?

studies.finding: Two double-blind experiments tested whether astrologers could match natal charts to personality profiles of unseen subjects.
studies.verdict: Matches stayed near the 33% chance rate, below astrologers' own predicted 50%.

claim: Did you know… the full moon drives up births, crime and psychiatric trouble?

studies.finding: Meta-analyzed 37 lunar studies and found moon phase accounted for no more than about 1% of variance in behavior.
studies.verdict: The lunar hypothesis failed tests of replicability and predictability.

studies.cite: Waldhoer, Haidinger & Vutuc (2002), Gynecologic and Obstetric Investigation
studies.finding: Analyzed 2,760,362 Austrian births across 371 lunar cycles for a relationship between lunar phase and delivery numbers.
studies.verdict: No significant lunar effect, even adjusting for parity and gestation.

claim: Did you know… dog bites surge when the moon is full?

studies.finding: Found animal-bite attendances at one English emergency department (1,621 patients, 1997-99) rose significantly around the full moon.
studies.verdict: A single-hospital finding; a rival analysis in the same issue disagreed.

studies.finding: Examined 1,671 dog-bite hospital admissions from 1997 to 1998 and found none of the 18 peak days fell on a full moon.
studies.verdict: No full-moon link; the largest peak was around New Year.

claim: Did you know… one identical personality sketch fits every student, rated 4.26 of 5?

studies.cite: Forer (1949), Journal of Abnormal and Social Psychology
studies.finding: Gave every student the same generic personality sketch and asked them to rate its accuracy; the class average was about 4.26 out of 5.
studies.verdict: Replicated for decades; effect appears in everyday horoscopes and readings.

studies.finding: Reviewed the Barnum literature, finding generic profiles are accepted more readily when labeled as personal and when favorable.
studies.verdict: Review supports the general finding across studies, mostly with college students.

claim: Did you know… healthy people can be made to feel outside their bodies?

studies.finding: Synchronized touch and a first-person camera view made volunteers feel located outside their own body, with skin-conductance responses to threat.
studies.verdict: Small samples, but the illusion is regularly reproduced in the lab.

studies.finding: Used virtual reality with conflicting visual and touch input so participants felt a virtual body was theirs and mislocated themselves.
studies.verdict: Bodily self-location is now studied experimentally as multisensory processing.

studies.finding: Reported a perceptual illusion of swapping bodies with another body viewed from a first-person perspective.
studies.verdict: Extended the effect to full body-swapping; the same laboratory's work.
